payload.name: segmental-bronchus
payload.scope: People made the segmental-bronchus construct to name each airway branch that supplies a single bronchopulmonary segment, so that thoracic surgeons can resect discrete lung units and bronchoscopists can target individual segments.

definition.body: The segmental-bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps each airway branch supplying a single bronchopulmonary segment, arising as a division of the lobar bronchus. Parameters: (1) the generational position — each segmental bronchus branches from its parent lobar or main bronchus at approximately the 4th to 5th generation from the carina, with 10 on the right and 8 to 10 on the left; (2) the cartilaginous support — irregular hyaline cartilage plates persist in the wall, fewer than in the lobar generation but more than in the subsegmental, maintaining airway patency; (3) the epithelial lining — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, continuous with the lobar bronchial lining and transitioning distally toward simple cuboidal; (4) the segmental supply — each segmental bronchus supplies a discrete bronchopulmonary segment, a functionally independent unit of lung parenchyma with its own vascular supply; (5) the bronchoscopic reach — each segmental bronchus ostium is directly reachable by flexible bronchoscopy, making them the primary targets for segmental interventions. It persists as a maintained landmark in thoracic surgery, pulmonology, radiology, and anatomical teaching. e.g.: the segmental bronchus as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; segmental bronchus targeting for endobronchial valve placement in emphysema treatment; bronchopulmonary segmental anatomy in Shackelford's Surgery of the Esophagus and Thorax, 3rd edition | not: the lobar-bronchus (the larger branch from which segmental bronchi diverge, proximal structure); the subsegmental-bronchus (the smaller branch distal to the segmental bronchus, without a discrete parenchymal unit) [formal: bronchus segmentalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.note: segmental-bronchus is a specific cartilage-bearing airway branch within the broader bronchiole category. The bronchiole definition (accepted) maps 'cartilage-free airway branches distal to the segmental bronchi,' explicitly distinguishing bronchioles from bronchi by the presence or absence of hyaline cartilage. payload.name: pulmonary-lobule
payload.scope: People made the pulmonary-lobule construct to partition each lung lobe into small pyramidal units bounded by connective tissue septa, so that pathologists can localize disease to a discrete structural unit and radiologists can interpret septal patterns on CT.

definition.body: The pulmonary lobule is a human-authored anatomical construct that partitions each pulmonary lobe into discrete pyramidal units with their apices directed toward the pleura. Parameters: (1) the boundary — the lobule is delimited by connective tissue septa extending from the visceral pleura into the lung parenchyma, dividing each lobe into approximately 50 to 100 lobules; (2) the central structure — a terminal bronchiole with its accompanying pulmonary artery branch runs through the center of the lobule, while lymphatics and veins occupy the peripheral septa; (3) the geometry — the lobule is pyramidal or polygonal in cross-section, approximately 1 to 2.5 cm in diameter, with its base toward the hilum and apex at the pleural surface; (4) the functional unit — each lobule is a self-contained ventilation and perfusion unit, with inflammatory patterns centered on the central bronchiole in diseases such as respiratory bronchiolitis and follicular bronchiolitis. It persists as a maintained landmark in pulmonary pathology, high-resolution CT interpretation, and anatomical teaching. e.g.: secondary pulmonary lobules visible as polygonal units on high-resolution CT; peribronchiolar granulomas in a sarcoidosis biopsy specimen; the wedge-shaped subpleural infarct of pulmonary thromboembolism | not: the pulmonary acinus (the finer gas-exchange unit nested inside a lobule); the pulmonary lobe (the larger organ division containing many lobules, bounded by fissures) [formal: lobulus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: alveolar-capillary-membrane
payload.scope: People made the alveolar-capillary-membrane construct to identify the diffusion barrier between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood, so that physiologists can compute gas exchange and pathologists can assess thickening in disease.

definition.body: The alveolar-capillary membrane is a human-authored anatomical construct that delineates the barrier through which oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood. Parameters: (1) the layered structure — the barrier comprises alveolar epithelium (type I pneumocyte), the fused basal lamina of epithelium and endothelium, and capillary endothelium; (2) the thickness — the thinnest point of the barrier measures 0.2 to 0.5 micrometers, a dimension critical to Fick diffusion, as measured by electron microscopy of human lung tissue; (3) the surface area — the gas-exchange surface spans approximately 70 square meters in the adult lung, partitioned into discrete alveolar-capillary units; (4) the clinical measure — thickening of the barrier from edema, fibrosis, or inflammation reduces diffusing capacity (DLCO), the standard noninvasive index of barrier integrity described in the ATS/ERS statement on respiratory function testing. It persists as a maintained construct in pulmonary physiology, histology, and critical care. e.g.: the barrier thickness measured by electron microscopy in West's Respiratory Physiology; DLCO reduction in pulmonary fibrosis per the ATS/ERS guidelines; interstitial lung disease showing basement membrane thickening on lung biopsy | not: the bronchial mucosa (the conducting airway lining proximal to the alveolar membrane); the blood-brain barrier (the endothelial barrier in cerebral microvasculature, anatomically distinct) [formal: membrana alveolo-capillaris | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vital-capacity
payload.scope: People made the vital-capacity construct to measure the maximum volume of air a person can expel from the lungs after a maximal inhalation, so that clinicians can classify obstructive and restrictive ventilatory defects and track pulmonary disease progression.

definition.body: The vital-capacity is a human-authored physiological construct that quantifies the maximum volume of air that can be voluntarily exhaled from the lungs following a maximal inspiration. Parameters: (1) the measurement — vital capacity equals total lung capacity minus residual volume, obtained by spirometry as the difference between the peak inspiratory volume and the lowest achievable expiratory volume; (2) the reference equations — predicted normal values are calculated from age, height, sex, and ethnicity using standard reference equations such as those from the NHANES survey, with results expressed as a percentage of predicted; (3) the classification role — vital capacity below 80 percent predicted indicates restrictive ventilatory impairment when paired with reduced total lung capacity, and a reduced forced vital capacity combined with an elevated FEV1/FVC ratio confirms restriction per the ATS/ERS spirometry statement; (4) the clinical uses — vital capacity guides preoperative pulmonary risk assessment, monitors disease progression in neuromuscular disorders where values below one liter predict respiratory failure, and quantifies improvement after bronchodilator therapy. It persists as a maintained spirometric standard in clinical pulmonology, occupational medicine, and respiratory physiology. e.g.: ATS/ERS spirometry showing vital capacity of 2.8 liters at 32 percent predicted; NHANES reference equations calculating expected vital capacity for a 45-year-old male; the vital capacity of 0.8 liters predicting mechanical ventilation in Guillain-Barre syndrome | not: the total lung capacity (the larger volume including residual air that cannot be expelled); the residual volume (the air remaining after maximal exhalation, not part of vital capacity) [formal: capacitas vitalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Param (3) gives predicted normal pulmonary capillary blood volume of approximately 70 to 100 mL at functional residual capacity, as determined by the single-breath carbon monoxide diffusing capacity method described by the ATS/ERS statement, and example 2 anchors the same value (the 70 mL normal pulmonary capillary blood volume from the DLCO reference equations in the ATS/ERS statement). The single-breath CO (Roughton-Forster) analysis gives a resting capillary blood volume of roughly 30 to 40 mL, classically about 32; 70 to 100 mL is the total pulmonary blood volume range, and the ATS/ERS DLCO statement's reference equations predict DLCO and DLCO/VA, not capillary blood volume. The filer's own example 1 cites West's Respiratory Physiology for the membrane - the standard source for the 32 mL figure. Anything cited real fails under item 5, and example 2, which carries the same figure, is not a real instance under item 7. The boundary carve (peritalveolar vs bronchial vs systemic) and the persistence line are a proper map carve; the error is local, but the wrong number sits in the carve body, which a later CORRECT cannot reach - the strike while provisional is the cheaper door.

payload.name: main-bronchus
payload.scope: People made the main-bronchus construct to name the two primary airway passages at the tracheal bifurcation, so that clinicians can distinguish the right and left airways for bronchoscopy, surgery, and aspiration management.

definition.body: The main-bronchus construct is a human-authored anatomical category that maps the two primary airway passages branching from the tracheal bifurcation (carina) into the right and left lungs. Parameters: (1) the pair — the right main bronchus, which is shorter, wider, and runs more vertically; the left main bronchus, which is longer, narrower, and runs more horizontally; (2) the anatomical course — extending from the carina at the T4–T5 vertebral level to the point where each enters its respective lung at the hilum and divides into lobar bronchi; (3) the wall structure — lined by the same pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium as the trachea, supported by hyaline cartilage plates in the right wall, with a smooth muscle layer (muscle of bronchus) between cartilage segments; (4) the clinical significance — the right main bronchus is the more common site of aspirated foreign bodies because of its steeper angle, and the main bronchi are key landmarks in bronchoscopy and thoracic surgery. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, thoracic surgery, and respiratory medicine. e.g.: the right main bronchus as the landmark for right upper lobe bronchus ostium in bronchoscopic atlases; the left main bronchus spanning ~6 cm beneath the aortic arch per Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; main bronchus stenting for malignant airway obstruction described in the Annals of Thoracic Surgery | not: the trachea (the single tubular airway above the carina, not a bifurcated pair); the lobar bronchus (the secondary branch distal to the main bronchus, arising within the lung hilum) [formal: bronchus primarius | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, thoracic surgery, and respiratory medicine. e.g.: the right main bronchus as the landmark for right upper lobe bronchus ostium in bronchoscopic atlases; the left main bronchus spanning ~6 cm beneath the aortic arch per Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; main bronchus stenting for malignant airway obstruction described in the Annals of Thoracic Surgery | not: the trachea (the single tubular airway above the carina, not a bifurcated pair); the lobar bronchus (the secondary branch distal to the main bronchus, arising within the lung hilum) [formal: bronchus primarius | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: People made the right-main-bronchus construct to name the wider, shorter, more vertical primary airway entering the right lung, so that surgeons and bronchoscopists can navigate the asymmetric airway and clinicians can manage aspiration.

definition.body: The right-main-bronchus construct is a human-authored anatomical category that maps the right primary airway passage branching from the tracheal bifurcation into the right lung. Parameters: (1) the course — extending from the carina at T4–T5 to the right pulmonary hilum, running shorter (~2.5 cm), wider, and more vertically than the left main bronchus at an angle of approximately 25° from the tracheal axis; (2) the wall structure — lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, supported by 6–10 irregular hyaline cartilage plates; (3) the branch pattern — giving rise to the right upper lobe bronchus before the hilum (the epibronchus), then dividing into intermediate bronchus and subsequently the middle and lower lobe bronchi; (4) the clinical significance — its steeper, wider path makes it the far more common site of aspirated foreign bodies (approximately 75% of cases), and its relationship to the azygos vein and esophagus is critical in thoracic surgery. It persists as a maintained landmark in bronchoscopy, thoracic surgery, and emergency medicine. e.g.: the right main bronchus as the preferred airway for unilateral intubation in trauma surgery; right main bronchus cannulation during ECMO circuit setup; bronchial stump fistula repair at the right main bronchial origin per the Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery | not: the trachea (the single airway above the carina); the right upper lobe bronchus (a tertiary branch arising from the right main bronchus before the hilum) [formal: bronchus primarius dexter | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pulmonary-artery
payload.scope: People made the pulmonary-artery construct to map the deoxygenated arterial pathway from the right ventricle to the pulmonary capillary beds, so that cardiologists, anesthesiologists, and vascular surgeons can assess pulmonary hypertension and plan catheter and surgical interventions.

definition.body: The pulmonary artery is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the arterial trunks carrying deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the capillary beds of both lungs. Parameters: (1) the pulmonary trunk, a single short trunk arising from the right ventricular outflow tract at the level of the sternal angle, dividing into the right and left pulmonary arteries before the hilum; (2) the right and left pulmonary arteries, each crossing into its hilum and dividing into lobar branches that follow the bronchi, with the left pulmonary artery passing over the left main bronchus; (3) the arterial wall, a muscular media with a prominent elastic lamina, thicker than the media of the companion pulmonary veins, built to accept the pressure of the right ventricle; (4) the hemodynamic access, the artery is the site of the wedge pressure measurement that stands in for left atrial pressure, and of the catheter that names the construct in hemodynamic monitoring. It persists as a defined anatomical landmark in cardiology, pulmonology, radiology, and anesthesiology. e.g.: four pulmonary arteries on transesophageal echocardiography per ASE guidelines; CT pulmonary angiography for pulmonary embolism in radiology practice; pulmonary artery catheter insertion for hemodynamic monitoring | not: the pulmonary vein (oxygenated return from the lungs to the left atrium, not an outflow artery); the bronchial artery (oxygenated systemic supply from the aorta, not deoxygenated outflow) [formal: arteria pulmonalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: bronchial-artery
payload.scope: People made the bronchial-artery construct to map the systemic arterial supply that carries oxygenated blood from the aorta to the bronchi and lung, so that interventional radiologists can embolize the source of massive hemoptysis and surgeons can control the bronchial circulation.

definition.body: The bronchial artery is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the systemic arterial branches that carry oxygenated blood from the descending thoracic aorta to the bronchi and the lung parenchyma. Parameters: (1) the origin, usually one left bronchial artery and one to three right bronchial arteries arising from the descending thoracic aorta, with origin and course that vary; (2) the course, the branches run down along the bronchial tree following the bronchi toward the segmental level, supplying the bronchial wall and the intersegmental parenchyma; (3) the wall, a muscular arterial wall, smaller in caliber with a thinner media than the companion pulmonary arteries of the same region, built for a low-flow systemic nutrient supply; (4) the clinical access, the bronchial arteries are the common source of massive hemoptysis, selectively catheterized and embolized for it, and the bronchial-to-pulmonary artery communication is a named pathological connection. It persists as a defined anatomical landmark in interventional radiology, thoracic surgery, pulmonology, and radiology. e.g.: bronchial artery embolization for hemoptysis per the Journal of Vascular and Interventional Radiology; bronchial artery anatomy on chest CT angiography; a bronchial-to-pulmonary artery fistula in a radiology atlas | not: the pulmonary artery (deoxygenated outflow from the right ventricle, not the systemic supply); the aorta (the systemic trunk of origin, not the branch to the lung) [formal: arteria bronchialis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: left-main-bronchus
payload.scope: People made the left-main-bronchus construct to name the narrower, longer, more horizontal primary airway entering the left lung, so that clinicians can distinguish left from right airway anatomy for bronchoscopy, aspiration management, and surgical planning.

definition.body: The left-main-bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the left primary airway passage branching from the tracheal bifurcation (carina) into the left lung. Parameters: (1) the course — extending from the carina at the T4-T5 vertebral level to the left pulmonary hilum, spanning approximately 4 to 6 cm, longer and narrower than the right main bronchus, and running at a more oblique angle of approximately 40-60 degrees from the tracheal axis; (2) the anatomical relationships — passing beneath the aortic arch at the level of the aortopulmonary window, and anterior to the esophagus and descending thoracic aorta; (3) the wall structure — lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, supported by irregular hyaline cartilage plates with a smooth muscle layer between plates; (4) the branch pattern — dividing into superior and inferior lobar bronchi within the left hilum, without an epibronchus, in contrast to the right main bronchus which gives rise to the right upper lobe bronchus before the hilum; (5) the clinical significance — the longer, more oblique course makes left main bronchus intubation more challenging than right, and the aortic impression on its anterior wall is a key landmark in thoracic surgery. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in bronchoscopy, thoracic surgery, and respiratory medicine. e.g.: the left main bronchus as the anatomical landmark for the aortic arch impression per Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; left main bronchus stenting for malignant obstruction described in the Annals of Thoracic Surgery; bronchoscopic navigation of the left main bronchus ostium for left upper lobe targeting | not: the right-main-bronchus (the shorter, more vertical contralateral airway); the trachea (the single airway above the carina, not one of the paired main bronchi) [formal: bronchus primarius sinister | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
